ami_style_notes:
The meeting has mostly medium-to-long turns during presentations, punctuated by very short acknowledgments, greetings, and transition cues from hosts and attendees. The opening is highly informal and overlapping, with frequent interruptions, side chatter, repeated greetings, and occasional audio/login troubleshooting; once talks begin, turn-taking becomes more orderly, with questions asked after each presentation. Speakers use many fillers and self-repairs—“um,” “yeah,” “okay,” repeated words, false starts, and loosely connected clauses—giving the exchange a spontaneous, conversational feel. Formality is collegial and academically professional but relaxed, with praise and personal rapport mixed into technical discussion. Questions are usually prefaced with compliments or hedges (“quick question,” “naive question,” “I’m curious”), then develop into multipart, exploratory prompts. Challenges are indirect and collaborative: participants frame alternatives as possibilities, ask for clarification, and build on prior answers rather than bluntly disputing claims. Responses tend to acknowledge the premise, qualify uncertainty, and think aloud through limitations, future work, or tentative interpretations.

Meeting style for this meeting (polite_friction): Courteous but with real tension. People disagree in an indirect way: with a question, a hedge, a long pause, or 'let's take that offline'. Some disagreements are dropped rather than resolved. Nobody raises their voice.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - I mean, that could work. I'd just want to see it on our data first.
  - Sure. We can park that and come back to it.
  - Right. I'd still like to know how you'd handle the late ones, but okay.
Opening: Start with a person asking for a quick catch-up because they missed the last meeting.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Choosing which retrofits to fund so older apartment buildings stay safe during multi-day heat waves.

speakers.name: Dr. Maya Srinivasan
speakers.background: Dr. Srinivasan is a building-performance engineer with 14 years of experience evaluating retrofit portfolios for multifamily housing, including naturally ventilated prewar buildings and affordable-housing modernization programs. Her work combines calibrated whole-building energy models, zone-level thermal simulation, heat-wave weather files, short-term indoor sensor deployments, and electrical load analysis. She has led studies of passive survivability, envelope measures, room air-conditioner sizing, and coincident peak demand under utility demand-response constraints.
speakers.distinct_perspective: She treats the buildings as coupled thermal and electrical systems. Her first question is whether a package keeps occupied rooms below exposure-relevant indoor temperature thresholds over consecutive hot nights, including during partial cooling failure or tenant non-use of equipment. She will propose candidate methods such as archetype-based EnergyPlus or equivalent dynamic simulations, calibration against interval utility data and monitored indoor temperatures where available, parametric testing of insulation, shading, glazing, cool roofs, cooling equipment, and panel capacity, and diversity-aware estimates of coincident demand. As project manager, she will push for a transparent package screen: technical feasibility, passive survivability, electrical readiness, peak-load implications, and uncertainty ranges rather than a single deterministic prediction.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Dr. Luis Herrera
speakers.background: Dr. Herrera is an environmental epidemiologist with 11 years of experience studying heat exposure among older adults, people with cardiovascular and respiratory conditions, and residents of low-income multifamily housing. He has designed tenant surveys, heat-wave cohort studies, indoor-temperature monitoring protocols, and mixed-methods evaluations of cooling access and emergency preparedness. His recent work links de-identified health-system and neighborhood surveillance data to weather indicators while emphasizing the limits of ecological inference.
speakers.distinct_perspective: He frames success as reducing harmful exposure for people, not simply lowering average building temperature or annual energy use. He will distinguish between outdoor heat, indoor conditions, cooling access, nighttime recovery, mobility limits, medical vulnerability, and whether residents can afford to operate cooling. He is likely to recommend a heat-health vulnerability framework that combines tenant survey data, age and chronic-condition risk strata, modeled or monitored indoor temperatures, and carefully selected health outcomes. He will insist that neighborhood emergency-department counts by age group can inform baseline burden and plausibility checks but cannot establish building-level causal retrofit effects. He will advocate for baseline and follow-up indoor monitoring, resident-reported access and behavior measures, pre-specified equity indicators, and cautious health-benefit modeling reviewed by epidemiologists and clinicians.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

speakers.name: Priya Nwosu
speakers.background: Priya is a fifth-year economics PhD candidate specializing in energy, housing, and public-policy evaluation. She has worked with utility billing records, landlord-tenant surveys, retrofit cost databases, and municipal program budgets. Her dissertation examines split incentives in rental housing and how electricity pricing, capital constraints, and imperfect information affect adoption of energy and resilience investments. She is experienced with lifecycle costing, sensitivity analysis, distributional incidence, and quasi-experimental research design, while recognizing the pilot's limited sample size.
speakers.distinct_perspective: She focuses on who pays, who benefits, and what the city gives up by choosing one package over another. She will ask for lifecycle costs rather than installed cost alone, including maintenance, replacement, tenant electricity bills, landlord costs, avoided emergency expenditures where defensible, and possible grid-capacity costs. She will propose candidate approaches such as a multi-criteria cost-effectiveness framework, distributional analysis by tenant vulnerability and bill responsibility, and scenario-based sensitivity analysis for energy prices, equipment use, heat-wave frequency, and discount rates. She will highlight the split-incentive problem: landlords may buy equipment while tenants bear operating costs, so a technically effective room-cooling option may not protect residents if it is too expensive to run. She will press the group to define a transparent prioritization rule, potentially using constrained optimization or ranked portfolios, but will question whether the available data can support strong causal claims about health savings.

speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

benchmark_task: Give an interdisciplinary meeting with enough research context for the evaluated AI to identify helpful methods from each discipline. Proposed reference methods must fit both the discipline and the research problem; expert review is needed.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Give an interdisciplinary meeting with enough research context for the evaluated AI to identify helpful methods from each discipline. Proposed reference methods must fit both the discipline and the research problem; expert review is needed.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Conduct a planning meeting among an environmental engineer, a public-health researcher, and an economist. The group should identify candidate methods each discipline can contribute to selecting heat-safety retrofits for the 24-building pilot, and should discuss how the methods can be connected in one decision process. The environmental engineer should describe methods for modeling indoor temperatures under multi-day heat waves, evaluating insulation, shading and cooling options, and estimating coincident electricity demand. The public-health researcher should describe methods for measuring or modeling heat exposure and heat-illness risk, including variation by age and cooling access, while noting that neighborhood emergency-department counts cannot by themselves establish building-level causal effects. The economist should describe methods for lifecycle and cost-effectiveness analysis, distributional or equity-sensitive analysis, and incentive analysis for split electricity bills. The meeting should settle on a proposed integrated analytic workflow and identify data or validation needs that remain unresolved. Do not claim that a particular retrofit is already optimal or that causal health effects are established from the available data. Methods should be presented as candidate approaches requiring disciplinary expert review, not as guaranteed conclusions.

environmental_engineering.method: Calibrated whole-building or representative-zone thermal simulation using local weather, building geometry, envelope characteristics, internal gains, ventilation and occupant-operation scenarios.
environmental_engineering.fit: Estimates indoor operative temperatures, hours above heat-safety thresholds, and performance of retrofit packages during three- to five-day heat waves.

environmental_engineering.method: Scenario-based energy and peak-demand modeling for efficient room cooling, common-area cooling and envelope measures.
environmental_engineering.fit: Quantifies electricity use and coincident grid load, including possible rebound or peak-demand effects of added cooling.

environmental_engineering.method: Building audit and monitoring protocol using indoor temperature and humidity loggers, with utility interval data where available.
environmental_engineering.fit: Supplies inputs and calibration/validation evidence for simulations and characterizes baseline overheating.

public_health.method: Heat-health risk assessment that links modeled or monitored indoor exposure metrics to vulnerability indicators such as age, chronic-condition proxies, mobility, cooling access and prior cooling-center use.
public_health.fit: Identifies which buildings and resident groups face the greatest health risk during indoor overheating.

public_health.method: Epidemiologic exposure-response modeling using heat-event, emergency-department and demographic data, with appropriate geographic and temporal aggregation.
public_health.fit: Provides a cautious basis for translating avoided indoor heat exposure into expected heat-illness benefits; neighborhood-level counts should not be treated as direct building-level causal evidence.

public_health.method: Prospective pilot evaluation with resident surveys and, where feasible, repeated health and behavior measures before and after retrofit implementation.
public_health.fit: Can assess cooling access, behavior, displacement to cooling centers, perceived heat strain and implementation effects; the design should account for confounding and selection into retrofit funding.

economics.method: Lifecycle cost analysis and cost-effectiveness analysis, such as cost per avoided heat-illness event or per heat-exposure reduction, using engineering outputs, health estimates, capital costs, maintenance costs and energy costs.
economics.fit: Allows competing retrofit packages to be compared under the limited pilot budget.

economics.method: Distributional cost-benefit or equity-weighted decision analysis.
economics.fit: Makes explicit how benefits and costs differ for high-risk residents, low-income tenants and landlords rather than relying only on aggregate efficiency.

economics.method: Principal-agent and incidence analysis of landlord-tenant split incentives, supplemented by sensitivity analysis of electricity tariffs, tenant bills, landlord costs and subsidy design.
economics.fit: Tests whether a technically effective retrofit will be adopted and whether its operating costs create burdens for tenants.

integrated_workflow: Audit buildings and collect or deploy baseline indoor-condition, utility, resident and cost data.
Use thermal and energy models, calibrated where possible with monitoring, to simulate candidate packages for representative heat-wave scenarios.
Convert modeled exposure changes into health-risk estimates using vulnerability-stratified public-health models and clearly state uncertainty and limits of causal inference.

Combine capital, maintenance, energy, health and distributional outcomes in a transparent multi-criteria decision analysis or constrained portfolio optimization that includes budget and peak-grid constraints.
Select pilot packages and buildings using pre-specified equity and performance criteria, then evaluate implementation prospectively to update models and funding rules.
unresolved_needs: Indoor temperature and humidity monitoring coverage, particularly in apartments occupied by high-risk residents.
Reliable building-level information on resident vulnerability, cooling access and tenant consent/privacy protections.
Local exposure-response assumptions suitable for indoor heat and the limits of using neighborhood emergency-department data.
Retrofit installation, maintenance, tariff and tenant-bill data needed for lifecycle and split-incentive analysis.
Expert review by environmental engineering, public-health and economics specialists before methods or results are used for funding decisions.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Srinivasan
transcript.text: Hi, everyone. Before we get going, a quick catch-up for anyone who missed the last one. We were leaning toward comparing retrofit packages at the building level, rather than treating each measure as a standalone purchase. For today, I’d like us to get specific about what counts as heat safety over a three- to five-day event, and how we screen packages for both indoor conditions and coincident electrical peak, because those can pull in different directions.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nwosu
transcript.text: Mm, okay.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Herrera
transcript.text: For me, heat safety has to include whether people can get through the nights, not just whether the building-average temperature drops. An older resident with heart or lung disease, or somebody rationing AC because of the bill, can still be at real risk in a package that looks good on average. I'd want indoor monitoring, plus a short resident measure of actual cooling use, affordability, and whether they had to leave home during the hottest hours.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Srinivasan
transcript.text: That’s the right distinction. For the model, I’d rather report occupied-room overnight exceedance, maybe hours above a threshold across successive nights, with operative temperature where we can, instead of a building mean. Then we can run cooling-use cases, including rationing and non-use. Luis, is the duration of those overnight excursions more, more useful to you than, say, the single hottest indoor hour?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Herrera
transcript.text: Duration is more useful, yes, especially when people can't cool down overnight for two or three nights. The hottest hour still matters for acute danger, but I'd track both- actually, I'd track peak exposure and cumulative hours above the threshold, stratified by residents who can't readily leave or who have cardiac or respiratory conditions. And Maya, can the model get us to apartment or room patterns instead of just occupied-room averages? The hottest top-floor, west-facing units may be where the health risk is concentrated.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Srinivasan
transcript.text: We can, though I'd frame it as representative apartment zones, not as a precise prediction for every unit. We can explicitly model top-floor and west-facing bedrooms with different window-opening and internal-gain schedules, then report the tail of the distribution, especially consecutive overnight exceedance under AC rationing or failure. The two top-floor walkthrough units we saw behaving so differently are exactly why I don't want envelope condition to stand in for occupant operation without some logger data.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nwosu
transcript.text: The rationing case matters for the comparison because a package that only works when residents can run room cooling freely may just shift the protection into a tenant bill they can't absorb. Maya, could your outputs separate cooling electricity and coincident evening peak under regular use, constrained use, and non-use? We need to see whether envelope measures buy enough safety to lower the operating-cost exposure, not just the modeled temperature.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Srinivasan
transcript.text: We can produce apartment cooling kWh, tenant-facing bill ranges, and a diversity-aware coincident demand estimate during the late-afternoon and evening peak for each package and operating case. So we're not just summing every unit's nameplate capacity. The uncertainty is the behavior assumption, frankly. I'd want Priya's view on what constrained-use cases are credible, and we need to check whether the interval data are actually fine-grained enough to anchor those load shapes.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nwosu
transcript.text: That would be really useful. For constrained use, I wouldn't infer it from low summer kWh alone. In the prior billing data, households reported hot bedrooms with almost no load increase, and we couldn't tell if that was efficiency, shared metering, or just not running the unit. Could we make the use cases explicit price-and-behavior scenarios, then check tariffs and arrearage risk before we attach bill ranges to them?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Srinivasan
transcript.text: I think we should keep the scenarios as inputs, not let the model quietly turn them into one behavioral forecast. No cooling, constrained use with a bill cap or limited hours, and regular use. Then the outputs can show which packages stay protective across those cases, and where protection depends on a tariff or subsidy. I’ll need to check the interval resolution and meter configuration before claiming we can validate the evening, evening load shapes.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Herrera
transcript.text: From the health side, I’d want those scenarios tied to what residents can actually sustain over all three to five days, not just a daily bill estimate. We’re already seeing people who technically have an AC but leave during hot afternoons, so the survey needs to ask if it’s cost, noise, safety, or whether the unit even works. I need to check how much of that we can collect without making the survey too intrusive.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Srinivasan
transcript.text: And that survey detail also helps us decide what “non-use” means in the thermal runs. If it’s cost-driven rationing, an envelope-plus-small-room-AC package may behave very differently than a unit that’s nonfunctional or too noisy to use overnight, so I don’t think we should collapse those. The monitoring question is which of the 24 can actually host bedroom loggers, because that’s our best check on those late-night patterns.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Herrera
transcript.text: Hm, bedroom loggers, yeah.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nwosu
transcript.text: The loggers matter, but I’d make sure we place some where the bill responsibility and vulnerability differ, not just in the thermally worst apartments. Otherwise we may learn a lot about exposure and still miss- we could still miss whether the package is usable for tenants who actually pay to operate it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Herrera
transcript.text: I'd make that a sampling rule, not just a nice-to-have. Cross the thermal-risk units with who pays the bill, age or health-risk proxies, and mobility or ability to leave. Otherwise, we could show a cooler bedroom in the worst-facing unit and still not know whether a frailer tenant elsewhere can afford to use the intervention through night three.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Srinivasan
transcript.text: That cross-stratification is non-negotiable. For the logger subset, I'd pair the vulnerability and bill-responsibility variables with a few physical strata. Top floor, solar exposure, and weak versus adequate electrical capacity. Then we'd use those observations to bound the representative-zone cases, not- we shouldn't pretend they're a random sample of all 24.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nwosu
transcript.text: And I'd add an economic stratum to that design. We need tenant-paid versus owner-paid electric and, ideally, households with some indication of bill stress. The package comparison should report not just exposure reduction but also the share of protection that depends on the tenant accepting a higher bill. Otherwise the apparent benefit is- it could partly be a cost transfer.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Srinivasan
transcript.text: I’d put that directly in the screen as a protection-contingency flag, not bury it in the narrative. A package can score well on modeled exposure only if the constrained-use case still holds. If it needs unrestricted tenant-paid cooling to stay below the overnight threshold, then that’s a different, different class of intervention, regardless of its annual-energy result.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Herrera
transcript.text: Right, that distinction matters.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nwosu
transcript.text: And that flag needs a financial counterpart. For each package, I'd show lifecycle cost separately for the city or landlord and for tenants. For tenants, that includes electricity, routine maintenance where it falls on them, and likely replacement assumptions. Then rank the packages under explicit tariff, heat-wave, and use scenarios. We should be careful not to monetize avoided health events too aggressively from neighborhood counts. Exposure reduction and affordability may be the more defensible primary outcomes here.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Srinivasan
transcript.text: Mm-hm. I agree we shouldn't lean too hard on monetized health benefits from those aggregate counts. For the engineering screen, I'd keep the primary result as the fraction of representative high-risk rooms that avoid cumulative overnight exceedance under each heat-wave and use scenario. Then show tenant bill exposure and coincident kW beside it. So a low-cost package can't look preferable because its unmet cooling need is invisible.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nwosu
transcript.text: Mm, that framing is clearer.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Herrera
transcript.text: I'd add one health-facing column to that screen. Not a dollar value, but the share of monitored or modeled high-risk bedrooms that achieve overnight recovery by night three, with the vulnerability strata visible. The neighborhood ED counts can tell us whether our heat-event pattern is plausible, but they should really stay a baseline-burden check, not evidence that one building package prevented cases.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Srinivasan
transcript.text: That works. I’d make the engineering criterion explicitly consecutive-night recovery in those representative bedrooms, alongside the worst-hour operative-temperature exceedance, because a package can pass one and fail the other. We’re at time, but I think the remaining practical check is which sites give us logger access and usable interval data. Without those, the uncertainty bands need to stay fairly wide.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nwosu
transcript.text: Yes—the uncertainty should be visible rather than averaged away.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Herrera
transcript.text: Yeah—visible uncertainty is important, especially for the highest-risk tenants.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Srinivasan
transcript.text: Okay, I’m going to give everyone a few minutes back. Thanks, this was really helpful. We’ll, uh, pick up on the site-data checks next time.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nwosu
transcript.text: Thank you, everyone. Goodbye.
